content: Promethazine can cause severe respiratory depression or cessation of breathing, which may result in death in children. It must not be administered to infants or children under 2 years of age and should be used with extreme caution in children aged 2 years or older. Promethazine should not be routinely used to treat vomiting in children and should only be prescribed in specific cases where a physician deems it necessary. Inform your child’s doctor if your child has any respiratory conditions, such as lung disease, asthma, or sleep apnea (a condition where breathing stops temporarily during sleep). You must inform your doctor or pharmacist about all medications your child is taking, especially barbiturates like phenobarbital (Luminal), medications for anxiety, narcotic pain relievers, sedatives, sleeping pills, and tranquilizers. Seek immediate medical attention if your child experiences difficulty breathing, wheezing, slowed or paused breathing, or stops breathing altogether. Discuss the risks of administering promethazine to your child with your doctor. Promethazine is prescribed to alleviate symptoms of allergic reactions, such as allergic rhinitis (runny nose and watery eyes caused by allergies to pollen, mold, or dust), allergic conjunctivitis (red, watery eyes due to allergies), allergic skin reactions, and allergic responses to blood or plasma products. It is also used in combination with other medications to treat anaphylaxis (a sudden, severe allergic reaction). Additionally, promethazine is used to sedate and relax patients before and after surgery, during labor, and at other times. It is also prescribed to prevent and manage nausea and vomiting after surgery and to help relieve post-surgical pain. Furthermore, it is used to prevent and treat motion sickness. Promethazine belongs to a class of medications called phenothiazines. It works by blocking the action of a specific natural substance in the body. When used to treat allergies, it is typically taken one to four times daily, before meals and/or at bedtime. For motion sickness, it is taken 30–60 minutes before travel and again after 8–12 hours if needed. On longer trips, it is usually taken in the morning and before the evening meal each day of travel. For nausea and vomiting, it is generally taken every 4–6 hours as needed. It may also be taken at bedtime the night before surgery to reduce anxiety and promote restful sleep. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take promethazine exactly as directed. Do not take more or less of it or take it more frequently than prescribed by your doctor. Promethazine suppositories are for rectal use only. Do not attempt to swallow the suppositories or insert them into any other part of your body. To insert a suppository, follow these steps: If the suppository feels soft, hold it under cold, running water for 1 minute. Remove the wrapper. Moisten the tip of the suppository with water. Lie on your left side and raise your right knee to your chest. (Left-handed individuals should lie on their right side and raise their left knee.) Using your finger, insert the suppository into the rectum, about 1/2 to 1 inch in children aged 2 years or older and 1 inch in adults. Hold it in place for a few moments. Stand up after about 15 minutes. Wash your hands thoroughly and resume your normal activities. This medication may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking promethazine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to promethazine, other phenothiazines (certain medications used to treat mental illness, nausea, vomiting, severe hiccups, and other conditions), or any other medications. Also, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you have ever had an unusual or unexpected reaction to promethazine, another phenothiazine, or any other medication. If you are unsure whether a medication you are allergic to is a phenothiazine, ask your doctor or pharmacist. Inform your doctor and pharmacist about all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking or plan to take. Be sure to mention any of the following: antidepressants (such as amitriptyline, amoxapine, clomipramine, desipramine, doxepin, imipramine, nortriptyline, protriptyline, and trimipramine), antihistamines, azathioprine, barbiturates (such as phenobarbital), cancer chemotherapy, epinephrine, ipratropium, medications for anxiety, irritable bowel disease, mental illness, motion sickness, Parkinson’s disease, seizures, ulcers, or urinary problems; monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) (such as isocarboxazid, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, and selegiline); narcotics and other pain medications; sedatives; sleeping pills; and tranquilizers. Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had an enlarged prostate, glaucoma, seizures, ulcers, blockages in the stomach or intestines, bladder blockages, asthma or other lung diseases, sleep apnea, cancer, or heart, kidney, or liver disease. If you are giving promethazine to a child, inform the child’s doctor if the child has any of the following symptoms before receiving the medication: vomiting, listlessness, drowsiness, confusion, aggression, seizures, yellowing of the skin or eyes, weakness, or flu-like symptoms. Also, inform the child’s doctor if the child has not been drinking fluids normally, has experienced excessive vomiting or diarrhea, or appears dehydrated. Inform your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. If you become pregnant while taking promethazine, contact your doctor. Do not breastfeed while taking promethazine. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform the doctor or dentist that you are taking promethazine. Be aware that this medication may cause drowsiness. Do not drive or operate machinery until you know how this medication affects you. If you are giving promethazine to a child, monitor the child to ensure they do not get injured while riding a bike or engaging in other potentially dangerous activities. Remember that alcohol can increase the drowsiness caused by this medication. Avoid unnecessary or prolonged exposure to sunlight and wear protective clothing, sunglasses, and sunscreen, as promethazine may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Promethazine can cause side effects. Inform your doctor if any of these symptoms are severe or persistent: dry mouth, drowsiness, listlessness, difficulty falling or staying asleep, nightmares, dizziness, ringing in the ears, blurred or double vision, loss of coordination, upset stomach, vomiting, nervousness, restlessness, hyperactivity, abnormally happy mood, stuffy nose, or itching. Some side effects can be serious. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of the following: wheezing, slowed breathing, temporary cessation of breathing, fever, sweating, stiff muscles, decreased alertness, fast or irregular heartbeat, fainting, abnormal or uncontrollable movements, hallucinations, confusion, overwhelming fear or emotion, seizures, uncontrollable shaking, unusual bruising or bleeding, sore throat, fever, chills, signs of infection, uncontrolled eye movements, tongue protrusion, abnormal neck position, inability to respond to others, yellowing of the skin or eyes, rash, hives, swelling of the face, eyes, lips, tongue, throat, arms, hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, hoarseness, or difficulty breathing or swallowing. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store this medication in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Store promethazine tablets and liquid at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Store promethazine suppositories in the refrigerator. Protect the medication from light. Dispose of any outdated or no longer needed medication. Consult your pharmacist about proper disposal. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the victim has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include difficulty breathing, slowed or stopped breathing, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, loss of consciousness, fast heartbeat, tight muscles, loss of coordination, continuous twisting movements of the hands and feet, dry mouth, wide pupils, flushing, upset stomach, constipation, abnormal excitement or agitation, and nightmares. Keep all appointments with your doctor. Promethazine may interfere with the results of home pregnancy tests. Consult your doctor if you think you might be pregnant while taking promethazine. Do not attempt to test for pregnancy at home. Before undergoing any laboratory tests, inform your doctor and laboratory personnel that you are taking promethazine. Do not share this medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have any questions about refilling your prescription.
